stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .124", Sentence = "The model shown in Figure 3, supplemented with three residual correlations, reproduced the correlation matrix of the Chinese sample reported by Ding et al. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: Using Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA), Ding et al. concluded that employees must experience sufficient satisfaction of their basic psychological needs at work in order to attain high levels of wellbeing.
However, necessity effects obtained with NCA can emerge even in the absence of genuine necessity relations because correlations between variables may create similar patterns.
In the present study, we reanalyzed the findings reported by Ding et al. by comparing the observed necessity effects with benchmark values expected from correlation alone.

Most of the reported effects (96.4%) were located within or below the estimated ranges of spuriousness, indicating that they were no larger than would be expected under conditions where no true necessity mechanism exists.
Consequently, the results reported by Ding et al. provide little support for the conclusion that psychological need satisfaction constitutes a necessary condition for employee well-being.
We argue that applications of NCA should routinely incorporate assessments of ranges of spuriousness and that necessity claims should be restricted to effects that clearly exceed these ranges.
Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA) evaluates potential necessity relationships by examining the extent of empty space in the upper-left part of an X-Y scatterplot.
The magnitude of this empty region is expressed relative to the total observed data space, defined by (Xmax -Xmin)(Ymax -Ymin).

According to the NCA framework, an absence of observations in this area implies that low values on X constrain the occurrence of high values on Y, thereby suggesting that X may be necessary for Y (Dul, 2016).

text.text: Their analyses focused on associations between selfreported satisfaction of the needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness at work and four indicators of employee well-being: job satisfaction, work meaningfulness, positive affect, and work engagement.

NCA yielded statistically significant necessity effects across the measures, leading the authors to conclude that "we found consistent support for the necessary role of psychological need satisfaction in all four well-being indicators" (p. 1) and, moreover, that "these findings advance our understanding of basic psychological needs through a necessity-oriented lens and underscore the importance of fostering a need-supportive work environment in organizations" (p. 1).
Such conclusions, however, depend on the assumption that observed NCA effects can be interpreted as evidence of necessity, an assumption that merits careful evaluation.
Research has shown that NCA can produce apparent necessity effects even when no true necessity relationship is present.

Empty regions in the upper-left section of a scatterplot can arise simply because two variables are correlated, and correlations themselves may be attributable to shared antecedents or other sources of confounding.
Accordingly, identifying a necessity effect through NCA does not, by itself, demonstrate necessity, just as finding a correlation does not establish causation (Sorjonen & Melin, 2025).

text.text: To address this issue, we previously proposed evaluating NCA results against ranges of spuriousness.
The procedure consists of generating a large number of datasets, for example 1,000, that reproduce the sample size and correlation observed in the original data but contain no necessity mechanism.
Necessity effects are then estimated for each simulated dataset, and a confidence interval is calculated across the resulting values.
This interval serves as a benchmark representing the magnitude of necessity effects that can be expected from correlation alone.
If an empirical effect falls within or below this interval, there is no evidence that it exceeds what would be anticipated in the absence of necessity.
In such cases, the hypothesis of a genuine necessity relationship should not be accepted.
The logic is analogous to the use of control groups in experimental research.
A treatment is not considered effective merely because it produces an outcome greater than zero; its effect must exceed what is observed under control conditions.

Similarly, necessity effects should be evaluated against what would be expected in data generated without any true necessity mechanism rather than against a null value of zero (Sorjonen & Melin, 2025).

text.text: Using this approach, we have previously found that reported necessity effects involving perceived burdensomeness and thwarted belonging in relation to suicidal ideation (Marchetti et al., 2026), as well as several proposed determinants of workplace creativity (Mercier & Lubart, 2026), were consistent with effects expected from correlation alone rather than reflecting genuine necessity relationships (Sorjonen et al., 2026a (Sorjonen et al., , 2026b)).

text.text: We applied the procedure outlined above to the findings reported by Ding et al.
Specifically, we generated 1,000 datasets corresponding to each reported sample size and observed correlation and then estimated the associated ranges of spuriousness.

Only two effects (3.6%), both involving the association between self-rated competence and self-rated work engagement in the UK sample, exceeded the benchmark expected from correlation alone.
Using the treatment-control analogy described above, this pattern resembles a situation in which the treatment group performs no better than the control group.
Given the limited evidence for genuine necessity effects, we explored a different explanation of the observed associations.
Specifically, we tested a model in which three observed variables function as indicators of need satisfaction at work and four observed variables function as indicators of employee well-being.
These two latent constructs were then specified as indicators of a higher-order general positivity factor.

Under this framework, correlations among the observed variables arise because they share common latent influences rather than because the variables exert direct causal or necessity effects on one another.

The model shown in Figure 3, supplemented with three residual correlations, reproduced the correlation matrix of the Chinese sample reported by Ding et al. (N = 345) with good fit (χ² = 15.2, df = 10, p = .124, CFI = 0.998, TLI = 0.995, RMSEA = .039 [90% CI: .000, .076], and SRMR = 0.009).

text.text: One residual correlation is particularly notable because it implies a negative relation between autonomy and work meaningfulness after controlling for the broader latent constructs.
Most importantly, the positive associations generated by the latent-factor structure are sufficient to produce the necessity effects detected by NCA.

Consequently, the findings reported by Ding et al. can be explained without assuming that any of the observed variables are necessary conditions for one another, raising the possibility that the reported necessity effects are spurious.
The present reanalysis evaluated the conclusion of Ding et al. that satisfaction of basic psychological needs at work represents a set of necessary conditions for employee well-being.
The findings indicate that nearly all reported necessity effects are no larger than those expected on the basis of correlations alone.
Accordingly, the available evidence provides little support for the claim that these variables stand in genuine necessity relationships.

Additional support for this interpretation comes from a latent-variable model that reproduces the observed correlation structure without invoking direct causal or necessity effects between the measured constructs.
Shared underlying factors appear sufficient to account for the observed pattern of associations and necessity effects.
Researchers using NCA should interpret statistically significant necessity effects with caution.
Correlation by itself can generate the characteristic empty-space patterns on which NCA is based.
Consequently, evidence from NCA should not be taken as proof of necessity unless the observed effects exceed those expected under appropriate non-necessity benchmarks.

We recommend that assessments of ranges of spuriousness become a standard component of NCA applications and that claims regarding necessary conditions be reserved for effects that surpass these thresholds.
The NCArigour function included in our analysis script (see link above) offers a straightforward means of implementing this evaluation procedure.
